name: Satellite and Cable Directive
evidence_rating: thin: Commission reviews only; no independent quantitative studies found
summary: The 1993 directive let satellite broadcasters clear rights only in their home country and made cable retransmission rights go through collecting societies. Commission reviews in 2002 and 2016 found these mechanisms eased cross-border TV, but rightholders kept licensing country by country and the rules did not reach online TV, where most broadcasters still geo-block. No independent study measures the effect on access, prices or revenues.

indicators.objective: The 1991 proposal has no indicators section; the Directive required a Commission report on its application

indicators.indicator: Country-of-origin rule for satellite broadcasts to ease rights clearance and cross-border reception
indicators.evidence: 2002 report: correctly transposed, but rightholders still license territorially (encryption), so practice is not in line with the country-of-origin principle. 2016 evaluation: mechanisms helped clear rights for satellite broadcasts, but are technology-specific and do not reach online transmission.

indicators.indicator: Mandatory collective management to clear retransmission rights
indicators.evidence: Reported as contributing to cross-border retransmission; some rightholders say they lose income; long mediation disputes.

indicators.indicator: Cross-border availability of broadcasters' online services
indicators.target_or_baseline: 82% of public and 62% of commercial broadcasters geo-block at least one online service (sector inquiry)
indicators.evidence: Led to Directive (EU) 2019/789; its review was due June 2025 (not found).

literature.citation: European Commission (2002), Report on the application of Council Directive 93/83/EEC (satellite broadcasting and cable retransmission), COM(2002) 430
literature.title: Report on the application of Council Directive 93/83/EEC (satellite broadcasting and cable retransmission)
literature.headline: Correct transposition everywhere, and the mechanisms contribute to cross-border TV broadcasting; but rightholders' practice (territorial licensing, encryption) is not in line with the country-of-origin principle; cable mediation slow; no extension of mandatory collective management proposed
literature.summary_plain: The first review found the directive's rules worked on paper and helped cross-border TV, but broadcasters still sold rights country by country and scrambled signals.

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Ex-post (REFIT) evaluation of the Satellite and Cable Directive (93/83/EEC), SWD(2016) 308
literature.title: Ex-post (REFIT) evaluation of the Satellite and Cable Directive (93/83/EEC)
literature.headline: Mechanisms helped clear rights for cross-border satellite broadcasts and simultaneous cable retransmission, but technology-specific provisions do not cover newer digital and online transmission; study data limited
literature.summary_plain: The 2016 evaluation found the directive eased rights clearing for satellite and cable, but its rules do not cover online TV.

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact assessment on the modernisation of EU copyright rules (online transmissions of broadcasters), SWD(2016) 301
literature.title: Impact assessment on the modernisation of EU copyright rules (online transmissions of broadcasters)
literature.headline: Country-of-origin approach not applied online; 82% of public and 62% of commercial broadcasters geo-block at least one online service (e-commerce sector inquiry); extending the principle to ancillary online services expected to widen cross-border access; commercial TV broadcasters warned of weaker territorial licensing
literature.summary_plain: The Commission found most broadcasters block their online services abroad and proposed extending the satellite rule online; commercial TV feared it would undermine exclusive licensing.
